analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax exemption to $2 million and expands a deduction for family-owned businesses.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 10, 2001 with one Republican cosponsor, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the amount of an estate shielded from the federal estate tax from roughly $700,000 to $1 million in 2002, climbing to $2 million by 2006. It would also let a surviving spouse use whatever portion of that exemption their deceased spouse never used, so a married couple could shield up to $4 million. Separately, it would raise a special estate tax deduction for qualified family-owned businesses from $675,000 to $3.375 million by 2006. The bill never advanced beyond the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth between roughly $700,000 and $2 million, widows and widowers who could inherit their spouse's unused exemption, and owners of family businesses and farms who could shield up to $3.375 million per spouse from estate tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of large estates and family businesses

how_it_helps.text: Raises the unified credit exclusion from $700,000 (the 2002 level) to $1 million in 2002, stepping up to $2 million for decedents dying in 2006 or later, which removes federal estate tax liability for estates at those sizes.
Adds spousal portability: a decedent's estate can use the unused portion of the immediately predeceased spouse's exclusion, so a married couple could shelter up to roughly $4 million.
Raises the maximum qualified family-owned business interest deduction from $675,000 to $875,000 in 2002, stepping up to $3.375 million by 2006, plus any unused spousal deduction amount.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Every estate that would have owed tax on value between the old and new thresholds no longer pays, so the revenue has to be replaced by other taxpayers or added to deficits. The benefit goes to a narrow set of large estates rather than being spread broadly.

drawbacks.text: The bill forgoes federal estate and gift tax revenue on estates up to $2 million ($4 million per married couple through the spousal transfer) and up to $3.375 million more for family businesses, shifting that burden to other taxpayers or the deficit.
The relief is concentrated on a small group. Only estates above the exclusion ever owed the tax, so the tax cut accrues to heirs of large estates rather than to working households generally.

The bill leaves the estate tax's top rates and structure untouched, so it offers nothing to the very largest estates and does not simplify the tax code; its higher family-business deduction comes with the same qualification requirements that made the existing $675,000 deduction difficult to use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real for a specific group: families facing estate tax on a moderately sized farm or business, where the tax can force a sale to pay the bill. Raising the exemption to $2 million with spousal portability is a moderate fix compared with full repeal, which the same Congress debated. The cost is forgone federal revenue borne by all taxpayers, and the benefit is concentrated on heirs of estates most working families will never have. It is a defensible targeted cut, but its gains flow upward.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Kent Conrad introduced the Estate Tax Reform Act of 2001 in the Senate on May 10, 2001, joined by Sen. Thad Cochran as an original cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.

The bill would have raised the estate and gift tax exclusion to $1 million in 2002 and $2 million by 2006, added transfer of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion, and raised the family-owned business deduction to $3.375 million by 2006.
No further action was ever taken: the committee scheduled no markup, the Senate held no vote, and the bill expired at the end of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal estate tax remained in place as it then stood, preserving the revenue for the Treasury and sparing general taxpayers from making it up. Heirs of large estates and owners of large family businesses did not get the added exemptions. The same Congress did enact a broader tax law that year which included its own estate tax changes, but this bill itself never moved.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 10, 2001 and took no further action; no markup or committee vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: There was no party-line vote to measure: a Democrat sponsored the bill and its only cosponsor was a Republican, but it never reached the floor, so party positions were never recorded.

industries.industry: Heirs of large estates and wealthy households
industries.note: The bill shields estates up to $2 million ($4 million per couple via spousal portability) from federal estate tax. The gain flows to heirs of large estates while the forgone revenue falls on general taxpayers.

Owners get a deduction rising to $3.375 million per spouse, easing estate taxes that can force heirs to sell a business. Defenders argue this keeps firms and jobs in the family, but the tax break still reduces public revenue.
Estate and gift tax revenue on estates between the old and new thresholds disappears, and it must be replaced by other taxes or borrowing.
